The company, the platform, the tenants and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the security analyst for the Kubernetes platform at Marrowby Credit Union, a fictional credit union. The database team rotated a password after seeing logins from an unknown Pod. Nobody can say who read the Secret: the cluster has no audit policy.
handover: Audit logging: off. Secrets: base64 in etcd, no encryption at rest configured.
The reporting namespace's ServiceAccount has a ClusterRole with list and get on secrets in all namespaces.
howItWorks: The console shows the alert queue, the event log and each asset's status.
Move on a check-in at a time. A decision comes to you at each check-in; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Check-in 2: the audit log, with every Secret's value, is indexed in the log platform that 200 people can search.
Check-in 3: the audit log now shows report-runner listing Secrets in five namespaces from a Pod the reporting team didn't deploy.
Check-in 4: a contractor's access to the backup bucket is found; every Secret in last night's backup is readable.

effects.log: Check-in 1: you need a trail from now on.

auditPrompt.title: Turn on auditing
auditPrompt.context: You will write an audit policy for the API server. Logs currently stay on the control plane nodes.

choices.label: An audit policy that logs Secrets and RBAC changes at Metadata (who, what, when, never the contents), skips noisy read-only system traffic, and ships the log to the SIEM

effects.log: Secret access is audited at Metadata and shipped off the nodes.

choices.feedback: Metadata records who read which Secret without writing its value into the log; shipping it off the control plane protects the trail.

choices.label: Metadata for everything, kept on the control plane nodes

effects.log: Everything is logged at Metadata, locally.

choices.feedback: The trail exists, but it is noisy and anyone who controls a control plane node can erase it.

choices.label: Log Secrets at RequestResponse so you can see exactly what was read

effects.log: Secret responses are written to the audit log.

choices.feedback: RequestResponse for Secrets copies every Secret's value into the audit log and everywhere it is shipped.

rbacPrompt.title: Read access to every Secret
rbacPrompt.context: The report job needs one Secret in its own namespace.

choices.label: Replace the ClusterRole binding with a Role in reporting allowing get on the one Secret by name, and turn off token automount where the API is not needed

effects.log: The account can read one Secret in its own namespace.

choices.feedback: Least privilege: one verb, one resource name, one namespace.

choices.label: Limit it to list and get on secrets in its own namespace

effects.log: Access is limited to its namespace.

choices.feedback: Much better, but list still exposes every Secret in reporting.

choices.label: Keep the access: reports may need more Secrets later
choices.feedback: Any compromise of the report Pod reads every credential in the cluster.

atRestPrompt.title: Base64 is not encryption
atRestPrompt.context: etcd backups go to a shared storage bucket nightly.

choices.label: Configure an encryption provider (KMS v2) for Secrets, then rewrite all existing Secrets so they are stored encrypted, and restrict the backup bucket

effects.log: Secrets are encrypted in etcd and in new backups.

choices.feedback: Encryption applies on write, so existing Secrets must be rewritten; backups then hold ciphertext.

choices.label: Configure encryption but don't rewrite existing Secrets

effects.log: Encryption is configured for new writes.

choices.feedback: Existing Secrets stay base64 until they are next written.

choices.label: Leave it: base64 already hides the values
choices.feedback: base64 is an encoding; anyone with a backup decodes every Secret in seconds.

scoring.modelReasoning: Kubernetes auditing records each request at a level set by policy: Metadata records who did what to which object without its contents, which is the level for Secrets; RequestResponse would copy Secret values into the log. Ship the log off the control plane. RBAC on Secrets should be get on named Secrets in the workload's namespace; list exposes them all. Secrets are only base64-encoded in etcd unless an encryption provider (KMS) is configured, and existing Secrets must be rewritten to be encrypted.
